questions.question: What becomes a transformer token in a standard Vision Transformer?
options: A pixel coordinate paired with a word
A flattened image patch
A convolutional feature map per class
A whole image caption
questions.explanation: ViT cuts the image into non-overlapping patches, flattens each patch’s pixel channels, and projects each vector to the model width. A caption is a possible output task, not the input token representation used by the patch encoder.

questions.question: A 224×224 image uses 16×16 non-overlapping patches. How many patch tokens are created?
options: 256 patches
14 patches
196 patches
224 patches
questions.explanation: Each side has 224 ÷ 16 = 14 patches, so the grid contains 14 × 14 = 196 patch tokens. The 224 value is the image side length; it is not the count of patches, and [CLS] is additional.

questions.question: What is the usual role of the prepended [CLS] token in ViT classification?
options: Its final hidden state summarizes the image
It replaces every patch positional embedding
It stores the first patch’s raw pixel values
It marks the start of a caption decoder
questions.explanation: For classification, ViT uses the final [CLS] hidden state as the image representation passed to a linear head. It does not hold a patch’s raw pixels; patch tokens carry the projected image regions.

questions.question: What cost follows from reducing ViT patch size while holding image resolution fixed?
options: The same tokens with a larger class vocabulary
Fewer tokens and lower quadratic attention cost
More channels without changing sequence length
More tokens and higher quadratic attention cost
questions.explanation: With resolution fixed, halving patch width doubles patches along each axis and quadruples N; full self-attention then scales roughly as N². Smaller patches therefore mean more tokens and higher attention cost, not fewer.

questions.question: A dataset is small and no large pretraining set is available. Which lesson caveat matters when choosing ViT over a CNN?
options: ViT patch tokens eliminate the need for positional signals
ViT uses local convolution by default for each patch
ViT lacks CNN locality bias and needs more data
CNNs require more images because they lack spatial priors
questions.explanation: CNNs encode locality and translation-related priors, while ViT starts with global token attention and relies more on data to learn spatial structure. Thus limited training data weakens ViT’s advantage; CNNs do not lack spatial priors.

questions.question: A segmentation model needs denser spatial detail than ViT-B/16 provides. Which direction does the lesson suggest?
options: Pool the image to one [CLS] token before the head
Use larger patches such as 32×32 or 64×64
Remove all position embeddings from patch tokens
Use smaller patches such as 8×8 or 14×14
questions.explanation: Dense prediction needs finer patch granularity, and the lesson suggests 8×8 or 14×14 patches for segmentation. Larger 32×32 or 64×64 patches merge more pixels into each token and coarsen spatial detail.
